DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Continuity (of complaint); Delay (reporting injury); Evidence (inconsistencies); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (Board implicitly dealt with issue)
DecSummary: The worker appealed an Appeals Adjudicator decision that he did not sustain an injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment in October, 1983.  There were no witnesses and he did not report the incident until the next day.  He complained to the company nurse several times through December, 1983.  In January, 1984, he had an acute episode of pain and did not return to work until December, 1984.  The Tribunal decided that, although there were inconsistencies in the worker's evidence, there was an incident in October, 1983, and the inconsistencies were due to confusion and passage of time rather than fabrication. The Tribunal also found continuity of complaint and that the acute pain in January was related to the 1983 incident and to a 1962 compensable accident. The worker was entitled to temporary total benefits. On preliminary issues, the Tribunal decided that it had jurisdiction to consider whether there was injury by accident under any of the heads of the statutory definition, and that if there was an injury by accident, then it would not matter whether it was a new injury or a recurrence of an old injury even if the Appeals Adjudicator had ruled only on the question of a new accident.

DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator confirming entitlement to compensation for a knee injury.  The worker fell while descending from the cab of a railway engine.  The employer claimed that the worker's knee gave way because of a pre-existing condition and that the injury did not arise out of the course of employment.  The Tribunal decided that what happened was a chance event under s 1(1)(a)(ii) of the Act.  It was not necessary for the worker to catch his foot on the railway equipment. The evidence established that descending from the cab was awkward because of the narrow space and stair.  It was more likely than not that the awkward descent contributed to the worker falling when his knee gave way.  This was sufficient to establish an injury arising out of and in the course of employment.  The employer's appeal was denied.

Vicechair: R. Hartman
EmpMember: D. Mason
WkrMember: B. Cook
DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Preexisting condition (disc, degeneration); Disc, prolapsed
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement to benefits for lost time subsequent to Aug. 16, 1982, as well as coverage for surgery performed on Jan. 25, 1983. On July 6, 1969, the worker, while employed as a cook in a restaurant, slipped on a wet floor and landed on her back. A July 7th examination disclosed pain and tenderness in the back region and over the left buttock and leg, and a diagnosis of a bruised lumbosacral spine, buttock and leg. The worker received temporary total compensation benefits for a period of time in 1970 and was later awarded a 15% permanent disability pension. The worker resumed regular employment in 1971. In April 1982, the worker was off work for one week, because of pain at the bottom of her spine radiating down her left leg. On Jan. 15, 1983, surgery was performed for a prolapsed disc. A review of the worker's file by the medical staff of the WCB noted that the worker had degenerative disc disease prior to 1969. In reviewing the medical evidence the Tribunal noted that there was no definite diagnosis with respect to the worker's spine either before or immediately subsequent to the accident in 1969. A firm diagnosis was not made until 1982. The Tribunal noted that medical evidence confirmed that the worker had ongoing back problems in the lumbosacral area of the spine. Noting that the inter-relationship of the pre-existing problems tentatively diagnosed and the compensable accident in 1969 cannot be overlooked, the Tribunal decided that, on the balance of probabilities, the surgery in 1983 was at least in part a result of the compensable accident. The appeal was allowed and the matter referred to the WCB for determination of the benefits.

DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\523_86.PDF
Vicechair: L. Bradbury
EmpMember: D. Mason
WkrMember: N. McCombie
DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for a low back disability. On Aug. 6, 1981, while at work, the worker slipped and fell striking his left buttock and elbow. The next day he felt pain in his neck and left shoulder, for which he received continuing treatment. Around August or September 1982, the worker began to experience pain in his lower back and left leg. In October 1982, a myelogram revealed a ruptured disc in his lower back. On Dec. 13, 1982, the worker had a laminectomy. Subsequently, the worker had an anterior cervical disectomy and fusion for his neck disability. The worker received compensation for his neck surgery and shoulder disability. Entitlement was denied for the low back disability and back surgery, since the delay of the onset of symptoms and delay in treatment made it difficult to establish a relationship between the back disability and the 1981 work accident. The Tribunal, after examining conflicting medical opinions, found that it was more probable than not that the worker's low back disability and resulting back surgery resulted from his work accident. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and referred the matter to the WCB for a determination as to the level of benefits.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant brought a s. 15 application to prevent the plaintiff from suing him for damages arising from a motor vehicle accident.  The plaintiff was a schedule 1 employee.  The issue was whether the defendant was in the course of his employment at the time of the accident.  The defendant was self-employed and had registered an aluminum siding company.  He also did other work such as home renovation and installation of car radios.  By application, the defendant was deemed to be a worker and at the time of the accident, he was receiving full compensation benefits for a previous accident.  The Tribunal found that the defendant was travelling from one store to another business contact.  He was both employer and employee and was in the course of employment at the time of the accident as he was travelling for business purposes.  It would be open for the WCB to consider whether the defendant's activities affected his right to full benefits for the previous accident, but this did not affect the issue before the Tribunal.  Also, the type of activity the defendant undertook would determine the assessment group for his company but would not affect his status as an employee.  The application was allowed.

DecSummary: The worker appealed two decisions of Appeals Adjudicators denying benefits from March 1983 to January 1984. The worker claimed that her 1983 disability resulted from a compensable 1975 accident which triggered degenerative disc disease, and from a transfer within the company to heavier work in Dec. 1982. The Tribunal reviewed conflicting medical reports and accepted the evidence that the 1975 accident made symptomatic an underlying degenerative condition from which the worker never recovered. This, together with the heavier work after Dec. 1982, resulted in a disability constituting disablement within the definition of s. 1(1)(a)(iii). Although the worker was capable of returning to light work in July, 1983, the Tribunal granted full compensation for the entire period since the worker regularly contacted the employer to request work and had an expectation that work would become available as she was a long-standing employee. On a preliminary issue, the Tribunal refused the employer's request that the employer's doctor give evidence as a medical expert, since prior notice had not been given. Therefore, it was not necessary to determine whether a company doctor could be qualified as a medical expert. It was also noted that Case Descriptions are marked as exhibits for purposes of identification and not as proof of the contents.

DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a WCB Appeal Board decision denying benefits for a disability which she claimed was related to a compensable injury and she argued that there had not been a proper WCB claim investigation.  The Tribunal could not find any specific deficiency and, in any event, the worker had had the opportunity to produce evidence at the hearings.  She claimed the Appeal Board reached conclusions of fact which were not supported by the evidence.  The Tribunal found the Appeal Board did make errors drawing conclusions from co-worker's evidence about continuity of complaint.  The errors were minor rather than significant and not critical to the decision, where the decision made no reference to continuity of complaint, and where other (especially medical) evidence was not supportive of ongoing disability.  About continuity of medical treatment, the Tribunal found the Appeal Board findings were not inconsistent with one report of treatment dates.  There was no evidence for concluding two favourable reports in the WCB file had not been considered by the Appeal Board, though they were not referred to in the decision.  Thus there was not good reason to doubt the decision's correctness.

DecKeywords: Charter of Rights; Jurisdiction, constitutional (obligation to consider constitutional issues); Medical examination (employer request); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (medical examination) (employer request)
DecSummary: The employer brought a s. 21 application for an order compelling the worker to attend a medical examination. The worker opposed the application on the grounds s. 21 was of no force and effect as being inconsistent with s. 7 and s. 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Tribunal concluded that this was not a case where a determination of the Tribunal's jurisdiction to declare s. 21 of no force and effect was necessary or appropriate as a less intrusive remedy was available. Section 21(2) provided the Tribunal with authority and jurisdiction to refuse or to modify the order requested by the employer so as not to infringe a worker's Charter rights. It would be wrong to consider the invalidity of a section of the Workers' Compensation Act if the same results could be accomplished without affecting the validity of the section. The Tribunal directed a hearing of the application on its merits be reconvened.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (adequacy of representation); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Merits and justice; Notice of hearing; Parties (participation) (leave to appeal)
DecSummary: A worker sought leave to appeal a WCB Appeal Board decision on the grounds there was reason to doubt the correctness of the decision as she had not been represented at the hearing and the Board had not adequately considered all the facts in arriving at its decision. In denying the application, the Tribunal noted that the worker had the opportunity to seek representation at the onset of the hearing and declined to do so. A lack of representation will not by itself cause the Tribunal to doubt the correctness of the Board's decision as appeals are directed on the 'real merits and justice of the case', not on the skills of the representatives. The Tribunal found the Board had reviewed the evidence before it and whether another hearing panel may have given certain evidence less weight does not create a good reason to doubt the correctness of the decision. In addition, although the employer had not participated in the previous WCB hearings, the Tribunal is directed to notify the parties of record as to the appeal regardless of their earlier participation. A party whose interests may be affected by the outcome of a hearing is entitled to appear at the application for leave in accordance with the basic requirements of natural justice.

DecSummary: A millwright injured his back in a 1981 fall from a scaffold. He was admitted to the Downsview Rehabilitation Centre but was discharged two months later with the indication that he was much improved and should return to work.  The worker continued to suffer back pain on his return to work and after a period of self-treatment, he sought relief from a chiropractor.  The WCB refused to pay for this chiropractic treatment on the grounds the worker had totally recovered from the compensable accident and an x-ray indicated non-compensable degenerative disc disease.  On appeal to the Tribunal from a 1985 decision of the WCB Appeals Adjudicator the worker argued ongoing chiropractic treatment was necessary to continue work. He could only obtain other treatment forms during working hours and he did not want to lose any time from work.  Medical reports submitted by the worker's representative indicated the worker's problems were the result of his compensable accident. The Panel agreed and held the worker was entitled to reimbursement for ongoing chiropractic treatments as these treatments were necessary health care resulting from the accident.  The appeal was allowed. The Panel also agreed to pay costs of obtaining medical reports as the reports contained information helpful in determining the matter.

EmpMember: D. Jago
WkrMember: N. McCombie
DecKeywords: Availability for employment; Merits and justice; Rehabilitation (cooperation); Rehabilitation, vocational (job search)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left wrist injury while at work on November 14, 1980.  The employer appealed the Appeals Adjudicator's decision that she was entitled to full temporary total benefits for the period of March 22, 1984 to November 29, 1984 as she had met the provisions of s. 41(1)(b).  The Tribunal noted that s. 41 must be viewed as a guideline for the exercise of discretion inherent in the section.  If a strict interpretation is given, a worker may be found to have failed one provision precisely because she followed the other.  The section is intended to ensure that workers take the steps available to them to assist them to get back to work, the real merits and justice of the case and the individual circumstances must be considered.  In this case, the worker had undertaken rehabilitation which understandably limited her job search.  The worker was a credible witness.  The Tribunal denied the employer's appeal as the worker had met the provisions of s. 41.

DecSummary: Pursuant to S. 77 of the Workers' Compensation Act, the worker appealed a decision of the Decision Review Branch allowing her employer access to her medical records. The Tribunal granted access to the information as it was relevant and necessary for the employer to adequately present its case and this need was not outweighed by prejudice to the worker. Access to relevant medical documentation should be granted unless there is substantial prejudice or embarrassment to the worker which far outweighs the significance of the material to the appeal. Section 77(7) requires the employer to protect the privacy of the worker after access to the medical records has been granted, and any contravention of ss. (7) is an offence under s. 77(8). Disclosure of information should not be prevented because one party deems it inaccurate as there is an opportunity to correct any inaccuracies at the hearing.

DecSummary: The worker, a yardman, suffered discomfort in both his back and hip regions in December 1978 when he slipped between a moving railway car and a walkway. DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable injury to his back in December 1965 for which he received a 10% permanent pension in April 1971. After 1971, he did not seek further medical attention until Nov. 1978, when he suffered strained ligaments and muscles of the lower back while lifting rocks for another employer. He received 3 weeks compensation. In Nov. 1984, the worker experienced radiating pain upon awaking one morning and was diagnosed in Feb. 1985 as having a degenerative disc disease. The Appeals Adjudicator disallowed the worker's claim for temporary total benefits on the basis that the Nov. 1984 pain was not related to the 1965 and 1978 compensable accidents. The Tribunal agreed and dismissed the appeal. Evidence indicated that the degenerative disc disease, first diagnosed in 1969, developed independently of the 1965 injury and that by 1971 the 1965 injury had stabilized. The 1978 injury was treated not as a recurrence of the 1965 injury but as a temporary aggravation of the degenerative disc disease. In addition, the worker did not lose time from work during the 1978 to 1984 period. The Tribunal stated that the 1978 injury did not aggravate the degenerative disc disease more than temporarily, nor did it accelerate its course. The Tribunal noted that degenerative disc disease may be caused or aggravated by a number of wear and tear factors.

Vicechair: J. Thomas
EmpMember: J. Connor
WkrMember: D. Beattie
DecKeywords: Election; In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue; Schedule 2 employer
DecSummary: The female plaintiff and the male plaintiff were passengers in their Schedule 1 employer's truck when it was struck by a train. The train was driven by a Schedule 2 employee while in the course of his employment. Both the employer and the male plaintiff were killed in the collision. Section 15 applications were brought to determine whether the plaintiffs' rights of action against their employer and the railway were taken away by s. 8(9). The evidence before the Tribunal indicated that although the employer intended to make a delivery of lumber during the road trip, the plaintiffs were travelling in the truck for personal reasons. For a worker to be in the course of his employment the worker must be engaged in the performance of a duty for the employer or doing something incidental thereto. The evidence was sufficient to conclude the plaintiffs were not in the course of their employment when the accident occurred. Therefore, although the female plaintiff had made an election s. 8(1) to receive benefits, the election was not valid, nor did it extinguish her right of action against the Schedule 2 employer. To make such an election did not bring something outside of the course of employment into the course of employment. The rights of action were not taken away by the Act.

EmpMember: D. Mason

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (dual purpose test); In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiffs Kaminski were co-owners of a lodge 100 miles outside of Thunder Bay. On Aug. 23, 1984, while en route to Thunder Bay, the female plaintiff, her three grandchildren and a lodge employee, the plaintiff Penassi, were involved in an auto collision with the defendant Clark. The defendant was a worker of a Schedule 1 employer and was in the course of his employment at the time of the accident. The female plaintiff was killed and two lawsuits were launched against the defendant Clark et al by Kaminski et al and Penassi for damages arising out of the accident. The defendant Clark brought an application under s. 15 of the Workers' Compensation Act, claiming that the plaintiffs' rights of action were taken away by s. 8(9) of the Act as they were in the course of their employment at the time of the accident. The Kaminskis had personal coverage under the Act through a s. 11 application. The Tribunal noted that although the plaintiff Kaminski had intended to do a few business errands in Thunder Bay, the trip was significantly a personal one as it was specifically arranged to drop the children off at the airport. Larson's dual purpose test, namely, did the trip involve the performance of a service for the employer which would have caused the trip to be taken even if it had not coincided with the personal purpose, was applied by the Tribunal in determining that a special trip to do the business errands would have been unnecessary. The plaintiff Penassi was on his day off and was travelling to Thunder Bay for personal reasons. In denying the defendant's application, the Tribunal found that the plaintiffs were not in the course of their employment at the time of the accident.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (permanent disability); Earnings basis (recurrences); Pensions (assessment) (recurring allergy)
DecSummary: In 1979 a worker who was an electronic assembler received compensation after developing a rash on her hands and lower arms from mixing epoxy resins. In 1981, she claimed compensation after a rash developed when she returned to work in an area adjacent to the epoxy mixing area. When the worker returned to work in 1982 in an area adjacent to the transducer area, she developed a third rash. Benefits were first denied for the third rash and then allowed as a recurrence of epoxy exposure. In 1983, the worker was assessed and awarded a 5% permanent partial pension on the basis the worker was unable to return to work where epoxy resins were being used. The worker objected to the earning basis used for calculation of her permanent pension. The worker argued that the rash she developed in 1979 was distinct and unconnected to the rashes she developed in 1981 and 1982. Awards of pensions should be based on the workers earnings 12 months prior to January 1982 (i.e. 1981 rather than 1978 earnings). The Tribunal, on the basis of medical opinion, concluded that the 1981 and 1982 outbreaks were recurrences of the 1979 condition. Under s. 43(1) and 122(6) where permanent disability results from an industrial disease, compensation shall be a payment not exceeding 75% of the worker's average weekly earnings during the 12 months immediately preceding the commencement of the disability.

EmpMember: J. Ronson
WkrMember: D. Beattie
DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The WCB Appeal Board denied a worker's claim for compensation for a lung disability, diagnosed as post-inflammatory fibrosis, on the ground that the disability did not result from the worker's employment.  The worker sought leave to appeal under s. 86o(3)(a) on the grounds that there was substantial new evidence at the hearing which was unavailable at the time of the WCB hearing .  He continued to seek medical attention for his condition which was becoming worse.  The worker relied upon two reports from a thoracic surgeon in his application.  The panel found that the new medical reports were new medical findings that differ from those at the time of the Appeal Board hearing and relate to the worker's condition of fibrosis. The panel concluded that the new evidence meets the tests set out in 86o(3)(a) and it is possible that the Appeal Board might have reached a different conclusion. Leave to appeal is granted by the panel.

Vicechair: J. Thomas
EmpMember: D. Jewell
WkrMember: N. McCombie
DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave under s. 86o(2) to appeal to the Tribunal from a decision of the WCB Appeal Board.  In the application before the Tribunal, the new evidence ground in s. 86o(3)(a) was relied upon.  The new evidence was an orthopaedic surgeon's report completed five years after the 1980 incident.  The Tribunal heard submissions concerning the tests or criteria that should be applied to interpret section 86o(3)(a) properly.  A review of the tests applied by our courts in considering when to re-open cases on the availability of new evidence was undertaken due to similarity to the statutory test in 86o(3)(a) but recognizing differences between court and compensation proceedings.  The Panel opted for a test not dissimilar to the position taken by the B.C. Workers' Compensation Board in Decision No. 29.  Although the orthopaedic surgeon's report of 1985 established a back injury, the panel held that taken in context of other evidence in the worker's file, it did not establish a likelihood of the Tribunal reaching a decision different from the one reached by the Appeal Board.  It did not explain how the 1980 work caused the worker's current complaints and contained no new medical theories or factual findings.  The application was dismissed.

DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\348_86.PDF
Vicechair: I. Strachan
EmpMember: J. Connor
WkrMember: S. Fox
DecKeywords: Psychotraumatic disability (phobia)
DecSummary: The worker received a 2% permanent disability award for her left arm which was fractured when caught in a conveyor belt on 14/07/83. Temporary total disability benefits ended in 02/84, at which time she was found fit to return to work. After the 1983 accident, she had been assessed by a psychometrist as suffering from a definite phobic condition resulting directly from the work accident. Her claim under s. 41 for continuation of temporary total disability benefits was denied on the basis that she had no psychotraumatic disability, only a fear of return to work with machinery. The Tribunal examined the evidence which indicated a credible phobia may amount to a psychotraumatic disability and be compensable under the Act. The worker's fear was genuine and during her partial disabililty she was actively seeking employment which she found on 30/06/84. The Tribunal concluded that the phobic reaction resulting from her injury had caused her to suffer a psychotraumatic disability which prevented her from returning to the accident employer or working with machinery. The Appeal for benefits between February 10, 1984 and June 30, 1984 was allowed.

DecKeywords: Accident (definition of); Arising out of employment; Causation; Injury by accident; Presumptions (entitlement); Significant contribution (of employment to injury)
DecSummary: A worker with no pre-existing weakness or disease experienced a sudden onset of sharp pain climbing into a fork-lift truck, an activity which normally has no adverse consequences.  He was disabled for two weeks by a torn calf muscle which the Tribunal held to be an injury by accident in that 'by accident' can mean either that the cause of an injury is unexpected or that the injury which results is unexpected. The Tribunal answered in the negative.

DecSummary: A worker appealed the decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying temporary total disability benefits for a 5 month period.  While working the night shift, she relieved another worker and was lifting a cookie box, weighing 25 pounds, when she injured her shoulder.  The worker received compensation benefits in 1984, but these were terminated at the end of 1985.  The worker believed she was unable to return to work despite the recommendation of Downsview Hospital and Rehabilitation Centre to return to work in order to get over her pain. DecSummary: Noting that the WCB's valid tests of continuity should not be too rigidly applied, the Tribunal granted entitlement of temporary benefits to a worker whose skull was seriously fractured in a 1958 work accident.  From 1958 to 1981, he had short sudden bursts of pain which did not disable him from working or cause him to seek treatment.  From late 1981 to April 1982, his headaches increased in length and severity, disabling him from work until they subsided.  The Tribunal accepted the opinion of his neurologist who ascribed the vascular headaches to the original injury rather than an intervening motor vehicle accident or other factors.

DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\72_86.PDF

EmpMember: D. Jago
WkrMember: L. Heard
DecKeywords: Accident (definition of); In the course of employment; Causation; Chance event; Injury by accident; Preexisting condition (disc, degeneration); Presumptions (entitlement); Sewing machine operator; Significant contribution (of employment to injury)
DecSummary: A sewing machine operator with pre-existing degenerative disc disease suffered a sudden unexpected escalation of pain symptoms, without misadventure, in the normal course of employment.  The Tribunal held that she suffered an 'injury by accident' in s. 3(1) as injury by accident includes a sudden unexpected injury during the course of worker's regular job, without an unusual movement, or an unexpected strain, or an external chance event.  In doing so, the Tribunal followed Re Kuntz and WCB and WCB v. Theed.  Since the injury occurred while she was working, her injury arose in the course of employment.  This finding triggered the presumption in (old) s. 3(2) that the injury arose out of her employment unless the contrary was shown.  In determining the nature of the employment's contribution to the injury, the Tribunal asked whether it could be shown that the employment made no significant contribution to the occurrence of the injury.  Although this question was inherently difficult as there was a related pre-existing disease and no obvious external employment-related cause, the Tribunal considered the evidence and answered in the negative.  The WCB was directed to determine the benefits.  The case-law on 'injury by accident' was analyzed in a technical appendix.

DecSummary: A s. 15 application was allowed and the plaintiff's right to sue was held to be taken away by Part 1 of the Act where 3 community college workers were killed in a motor vehicle collision.  The deceased were in the course of employment when driving in a straight forward manner to an out-of-town conference paid for by the college.  They did not take themselves out of the course of employment by first planning to attend a closely connected social event.  An obligation to travel on company business where the employer agrees to pay for the trip, is analogous to travelling employee cases rather than to employees going to and from work.  The college was properly added as a Schedule 1 employer when the WCB  accepted its 1966 application for inclusion under s. 95 of the Act.  A regulation which excludes an 'educational work' from part 1 of the Act, does not preclude an application for inclusion because, where a regulation and a statute conflict, the statute prevails.

DecKeywords: Action (derivative); Election; In the course of employment (travelling); Independent operator (truck driver); Scope of hearing; Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (right to sue); Parties (right to sue); Right to sue (professional negligence); Worker (test) (organization test)
DecSummary: The respondent/plaintiff was in a collision with a truck driver.  The truck driver was hired to haul freight in his own truck, but was delivering another truck for his employer for maintenance when the accident occurred.  The respondent subsequently sued his solicitor and the WCB for negligence in not suing the other driver.  The Tribunal applied the 'organization test' to hold that the other driver was an employee, not an independent contractor.  The respondent's right of action was taken away by s.8(9).  The Tribunal's jurisdiction was not lost because the applicant 'party' (ie the solicitor) was neither a worker nor an employer or because the action for professional negligence was in effect substituted for the original tort claim which was statute-barred.  Further, in a s.15 application, the Tribunal's responsibility is to decide both whether the plaintiff has a right to compensation (his employment status) and whether his right of action is taken away by s.8(9).  The Tribunal's responsibility is not limited to questions raised by the parties.

DecKeywords: Accident (definition of); Disablement (strenuous work); Board Directives and Guidelines (disablement) (specific incident)
DecSummary: A radiator repairman claimed compensation for a back disability which symptoms had increased immediately after a non-occupational incident.  Evidence was presented that his jobs for 11 years involved heavy lifting and bending.  Medical reports established a relationship between the work and the disability.  The worker complained of back pain prior to the incident.  Pursuant to s 1(1)(a)(iii), the Tribunal held that entitlement was established if the work process was shown to involve strenuous work or an awkward position and the disablement was causally related to the process.  While helpful, it is not necessary to prove a specific incident or a recent change in a longstanding work process.  Furthermore, the non-occupational incident was minor in nature and was only a triggering factor while the real cause of the disability arose out of and in the course of his employment.  The appeal was allowed.

DecSummary: Worker was granted entitlement by WCB Appeal Board for his back disability.  Following the WCB Appeal Board hearing and prior to rendering a decision, the Board obtained a medical report from an outside orthopaedic consultant.  On application to the Tribunal for leave to appeal, the employer argued that outside consultant had not received all the medical information in the file and therefore his opinion should not have been relied on by the WCB Appeal Board.  The Tribunal found that outside consultant had all the evidence on file.  The employer also contacted a specialist and requested his opinion after receipt of the Appeal Board's decision. The Tribunal concluded that the specialist's opinion would not constitute good reason to doubt the correctness of the Appeal Board's decision under s. 86o(3)(b) as it was not of sufficient weight for the Appeal Board to prefer it to the reports of other specialists. The Tribunal also found that, even if the application had been brought under s. 86o(3)(a) on substantial new evidence it would fail as the specialist's report was not substantial. In addition, the Tribunal felt the report could have been made available to the Appeal Board before this decision. The Panel denied leave to appeal.

She was off work for 2 weeks before she returned to work, fearing loss of this relatively light work assignment. DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\32_86.PDF
Vicechair: R. Ellis
EmpMember: D. Mason
WkrMember: S. Fox
DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Causation (disc, degeneration); Continuity (of complaint); Continuity (of treatment); Disc, degeneration
DecSummary: Worker seeking compensation in 1984 for degenerative disc disease. Question is whether there is a causal connection between disease and compensable injuries in 1966 and 1976. Medical reports were conflicting. Medical information presented showed a limited understanding by medicine of the cause of disc disease. Therefore the Tribunal must rely on actual evidence. For example, if a worker is symptom free before the strain and suffers continual pain afterwards then the strain is a probable cause. But if the symptoms subside shortly after the strain then the strain is not a significant factor. Sources of evidence include medical treatment received and evidence of complaints to supervisors, co-workers, friends and relatives. The worker presented evidence of medical treatment and WCB complaints form and testimony by wife and co-worker of complaints by worker. Based on evidence Tribunal was uncertain as to causal connection of 1976 injury but applied presumption of s. 3(4) resolved issue in favour of worker.

DecKeywords: Intervenors; Investigation by Tribunal; Scope of hearing; Issue setting; Pensions (assessment); Permanent disability; Procedure (leading case strategy); Standing; Summons (to Board doctor); Case Direction Panel
DecSummary: As described in the Pension Assessment Appeals Leading Case Practice Direction (Dec. 1985) the Tribunal adopted a leading case strategy for pension assessments. The leading case having been selected by a Case Direction Panel, a pre-hearing conference was held, attended by the parties and by others wishing to appear as intervenors. This Interim Report lists the organizations awarded intervenors status and discusses their role at the hearing. The Tribunal discusses its investigative and issue-setting functions and outlines the issues to be addressed at the appeal. These issues are: whether the cost of the worker's pension may be charged to the second injury and enhancement fund, the level of the pension, entitlement, the right to a supplement, the effective date of review, the meaning of s. 45(1), the rating schedule, the standard of review, the role of psychogenic pain in pension level assessment and retroactivity. A guide is provided for Tribunal counsel and the Case Direction Panel in developing the evidence to be presented regarding these issues.

DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\831L_86.PDF
Vicechair: N. Catton
EmpMember: B. Apsey
WkrMember: D. Beattie
DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation); Delay (leave to appeal); Discretion, Board (commutation); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (application of Board policy); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (discretion, Board)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a 1985 decision of the Appeal Board upholding the WCB's 1964 decision to commute the worker's pension.  In 1953 the worker suffered a serious leg injury for which he was awarded a 15% pension, paid at $14.75 per month.  In 1962, the WCB made an administrative decision to commute pensions of less than $15.00 per month.  Guidelines for determining whether a commutation would be to the permanent advantage of the worker included careful consideration of commutation of pensions greater than 10%, further consideration if the lump sum exceeded $2,500.00 and potential for deterioration of the compensable condition.  In 1964, the WCB commuted the worker's pension and paid him a lump sum of $3,200.  The Tribunal found that there was no error of law since the WCB had discretion under s.26 to commute pensions greater than 10%.  The delay by the worker was not unreasonable since he had relied on the WCB's expertise, and it was not until the late 1970's that the deterioration of his condition became known.  The fact that the worker's condition deteriorated does not necessarily mean the decision was incorrect.  However, there was no indication that the WCB considered and investigated the worker's condition in relation to the guidelines.  Therefore, there was good reason to doubt the correctness of the 1964 decision.  Further there was good reason to doubt the correctness of the Appeal Board decision because it failed to apply the facts to the policy in effect in 1964.  Leave to appeal was granted.

DecKeywords: Airline employment; Arising out of employment (takes self out of employment) (misconduct); In the course of employment (distinct departure test); In the course of employment (overnight accommodation); In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (reasonably incidental activity test); In the course of employment (travelling); Misconduct; Arising out of employment (travelling)
DecSummary: A flight attendant, walking from a restaurant to a cafe at 1:30 a.m. during a required layover in Amsterdam, suffered a concussion when she ran after a purse snatcher who attacked her. The employer argued she had taken herself out of the course of her employment after leaving the restaurant because she had embarked on activity for her own personal reasons and which was unnecessarily perilous. A majority of the Tribunal concluded that a 'reasonable activity' test was appropriate to apply to workers required to stay overnight in foreign locations. The employer recognized the importance of a degree of freedom on layovers by not requiring its workers to keep a supervisor constantly advised of their whereabouts. The layover in a foreign location and the fact that it was important to be out late to adjust to the time change exposed the worker to an increased risk. The majority held that in all the circumstances, her conduct bore a reasonable relationship to her employment, which resulted in an accident which arose out of and in the course of employment.

DecNum: MATTABI
DecFileName: http://www.wsiat.on.ca/Decisions/198586\MATTABI_86.PDF
Vicechair: J. Thomas
EmpMember: D. Mason
WkrMember: N. McCombie
DecKeywords: Notice of hearing; Procedure (consolidation); Right to sue
DecSummary: Thirty-three employees of a mining company were injured in an accident involving a bus operated by a leasing company and chartered by the employer.   Thirty-two workers originally elected to claim compensation and were awarded benefits.  One worker elected to sue the leasing company.  The Workers' Compensation Appeal Board ordered a rehearing by means of a s. 15 application to determine this worker's right to sue.  Three other workers subsequently commenced lawsuits which gave rise of s. 15 applications to determine the same issue.  The employer also appealed the appeals adjudicator's award of benefits to one employee based on a finding that the accident arose out of and in the course of employment.  In an interim ruling, an Appeals Tribunal case direction panel decided that the four s. 15 applications and the employer appeal arose out of the same accident and the issue of whether the accident arose out of and in the course of employment was relevant to them all.  The panel held that the Tribunal should consolidate proceedings arising out of the same accident wherever possible to minimize costs and avoid inconsistency.  The panel also directed that all workers injured in the same accident should be given notice of these proceedings , although they were not parties, due to their substantial interest in the outcome.

The worker started his job in 1974.  He claimed that he began to suffer from increasingly severe headaches in 1976.  He stopped working in 1979.  Shortly after discontinuing work, the worker began to suffer from the psychiatric condition.  The Tribunal reviewed studies regarding the correlation between high noise levels and hypertension and between high noise levels and psychological disorders. The studies on psychological disorders concerned exposure to air traffic noise, not conditions similar to those of the worker. The evidence did not support the claim.

DecSummary: Pursuant to leave granted in Decision No. 295, the worker appealed a decision of the WCB Appeal Board denying temporary total disability benefits beyond Oct. 13, 1983. In 1971, the worker suffered a compensable back injury, for which he was awarded a 20% pension. In 1980, the worker reinjured his back, for which he received temporary total benefits less pension. In Oct. 1983, benefits were terminated. The Tribunal found that there was medical evidence of organic injury in addition to psychological factors. The worker was not totally disabled after Oct. 1983. However, new evidence concerning organic injury was relevant to reassessing the worker's pension. On a preliminary issue, the Tribunal considered the standard of review in appeals pursuant to leave. It was submitted that the Tribunal had overturned the Appeal Board in the decision to grant leave to appeal, that the Tribunal was bound by its earlier decision, that the standard for this hearing on the merits could be no higher than that required for granting leave. It was argued that since the Appeal Board erred, the Tribunal should restore the worker to the position he would have been in by granting benefits from Oct. 1983. The Tribunal concluded that it would decide the case using the same standard as it does on all appeals, that is, the real merits and justice of the case. The appeal was allowed in part. The matter was remitted to the Board for reassessment of pension. The Tribunal recommended consideration of psychogenic pain in a treatment programme.

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement beyond Aug. 13, 1984. His benefits were terminated after he was discharged from PSEM in August 1984 with a discharge report that there was no organic basis for ongoing pain, and that his psychogenic pain was not related to the accident but rather was personality-engendered. DecSummary: The worker applied under s. 86o3(a) and (b) for leave to appeal a decision of the WCB Appeal Board denying entitlement for industrial disease. The worker was a miner who claimed to be suffering from silicosis. DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying benefits beyond June 8, 1984 for injuries suffered in a compensable accident in Nov. 1983. The worker was a construction worker who suffered numerous injuries including cervical and lumbar sprain when hit by a company truck. In May 1984, the worker was discharged from the Rehabilitation Centre with a recommendation to do modified work, avoiding heavy lifting, walking on rough ground and repetitive bending. On June 4, 1984, the worker returned to work and was given a job carrying planks which caused increased pain in his back and neck. He was given a lighter job which he did for one hour before being sent home. On June 18, he reported to work again. Although there was conflicting evidence as to what happened, it appeared that he was in pain and the lighter job may not have been offered to him. The Tribunal found that the worker was partially disabled. The job moving planks was not suitable, as it aggravated his condition and prevented him from doing the lighter job. On June 18, the worker may not have been capable of working and did not appear to have been offered suitable work. The Tribunal decided that the worker met the onus of taking steps to assist in getting back to work. He was available for work but no suitable work was provided. After June 18, he conducted a thorough job search until finding suitable employment in March 1986. The worker was entitled to full compensation. The appeal was allowed. A dissenting panel member felt there was no new evidence or information which would merit a decision different from that of the Appeals Adjudicator.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (maximum); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (error of law) (statutory interpretation); Personal coverage; Procedure (leave to appeal) (application and merits together)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the WCB Appeal Board allowing benefits for a compensable accident in 1971 based on earnings of only $7,000 per year. The worker started his own business in 1967 and applied for personal coverage. In August 1971 the maximum earnings under the Act was raised from $7,000 to $9,000. The worker paid assessments based on an estimated salary of $11,000. The Appeals Adjudicator stated that the new maximum would not take effect until the worker returned his 1972 assessment requesting maximum coverage. The Appeal Board agreed without giving reasons for not applying the maximum in effect at the time of the injury. The Tribunal decided that there was good reason to doubt the correctness of the decision, since it was contrary to the clear and unambiguous wording of the statute. It was clear also that the worker wanted coverage in excess of the prior $7,000 maximum, and therefore he was entitled to the new maximum of $9,000. Leave to appeal was granted. As this case involved a discrete yes or no issue, there was no need for another hearing, and the appeal was allowed. The Tribunal also determined that it did not have jurisdiction on issues of reimbursement of the portion of the assessment in excess of the maximum and interest on the extra benefits payable, since these had not been finally dealt with by the Board.

DecSummary: The worker applied under s. 86o(3)(a) and (b) for leave to appeal a decision and two reconsiderations of the WCB Appeal Board denying entitlement for the worker's respiratory problems.  The worker was a miner who claimed that his bronchial asthma was caused by inhalation of oil fumes in an underground work environment.  The worker submitted that scientific literature had become available linking inhalation of oil fumes to occupational lung disorders.  The Tribunal noted that, in considering an application for leave to appeal on the ground of substantial new evidence, the evidence relied upon must be before the Tribunal.  In this case, although the articles were not before the Tribunal, the Tribunal acquired them to ensure there was no prejudice to the worker.  The articles only established a possibility of a link.  The Tribunal was not satisfied that a different panel of the Tribunal considering this evidence would reach a different conclusion from that of the Appeal Board.  On the ground of good reason to doubt correctness, the Tribunal found that there was ample evidence to support the conclusion that the worker's bronchial condition was not caused by his employment.  However, the failure of the Appeal Board to consider entitlement on the basis of aggravation of a pre-existing respiratory condition was a critical error.  Leave to appeal was granted on this ground only.

Vicechair: A. Signoroni

DecKeywords: Arthritis; Continuity (of treatment); Delay (evidence); Estoppel (representation or conduct)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for knee, hip, shin and ankle conditions which the worker claimed were related to a compensable accident in 1968. In 1968, the worker injured his knee at work. On a doctor's recommendation, the worker had light duty for three weeks. A claim for medical aid was allowed. In 1972, the worker requested the WCB to reopen his claim. He complained of pain, and was given cortisone by an orthopaedic specialist. The WCB denied entitlement but paid the doctor's account, since the doctor's report assisted in adjudicating the claim. In 1984, the worker again requested the WCB to reopen the file. The Appeals Adjudicator concluded that the worker had arthritis unrelated to the 1968 accident. The Tribunal found no reason to disturb the Adjudicator's decision. The original injury in 1968 was a minor one, for which the worker did not lose time from work. There was a lack of treatment from 1968 to 1984, except for the cortisone injection in 1972. The payment of the doctor's account by the WCB in 1972 was not an implicit acceptance of entitlement. The failure of the Board in 1972, to seek additional evidence from the doctor who examined the worker after the accident was a concern, but the worker could have pursued that himself. There was insufficient evidence to establish a claim. In view of his delay, the worker could not claim prejudice from lack of evidence. The worker also claimed that he was not advised of his rights of appeal in 1972. The Tribunal found no linguistic or educational factors preventing him from seeking assistance. The appeal was denied.

Vicechair: R. Ellis
EmpMember: D. Jago
WkrMember: L. Heard
DecKeywords: Natural justice (opportunity to make submissions); Procedure (reconsideration) (constitution of Panel); Procedure (reconsideration) (role of Board); Reconsideration (change in law); Reconsideration (procedural error) (opportunity to make submissions); Standing (Board)
DecSummary: The WCB and the employer applied for a reconsideration of Decision 72. The employer applied for reconsideration on the grounds that it was not given an opportunity to make submissions regarding the interpretation of the words 'injury by accident' and the decision of the Divisional Court in Kuntz and Dagenais. Kuntz and Dagenais was mentioned at the hearing but the parties and the panel did not appreciate its significance until later. An issue arose as to the involvement of the original Panel which decided Decision 72 in the application for reconsideration. The Panel concluded that the same Panel should reconsider applications based on non-compliance with the principles of natural justice in the conduct of the Tribunal's process, just as a panel would consider a procedural complaint during the course of a hearing. On the merits of this ground, the panel decided that it should have given the parties an opportunity to make further submissions after the significance of Kuntz was appreciated. However, the Panel must still determine whether the omission in the proceedings amounted to a breach of the common law principles of natural justice of a kind that would lead a court to conclude that the panel had effectively acted beyond its jurisdiction. In this case, the Panel concluded that the process met the minimum standards of natural justice since the issue was mentioned at the hearing, the Kuntz decision was available and the employer could have made submissions at the hearing. In addition, the employer applied for reconsideration on the basis of the Court of Appeal decision in Kuntz and Dagenais which reversed the Divisional Court. In the absence of established procedure as to the role of the original panel in applications on grounds other than procedural fairness, the panel requested that a different panel consider whether Kuntz would provide appropriate or sufficient grounds for reconsideration, and if so whether the reconsideration should be by the original panel or a different panel. The last issue considered at this hearing was the Board's application for reconsideration. The Panel concluded that the Board did not have the right of standing in Tribunal proceedings. It is not appropriate for the Board to make applications for reconsideration. However, the Tribunal would continue to invite the Board to contribute to hearings by provident information or explanation and, in appropriate circumstances, would invite the Board to make advocacy-style submissions in support of its administrator's views as to issues concerning the interpretation of the policy and general law of the Act. The Tribunal could then consider the information and decide on its own whether to reconsider a decision. In this case, the Board was invited to participate in the employer's reconsideration for the purpose of providing information and to advocate the Board's view of personal injury by accident.

WkrMember: F. Lankin
DecKeywords: Chance event; Contractor (principal's liability for assessments); Election; Exposure (chemicals); In the course of employment (contemporaneity); Right to sue; Subcontractor; Worker (deemed)
DecSummary: Section 15 application to determine whether the worker's right of action was taken away.  The worker was employed by L&N as a mechanic servicing L&N's machinery. L&N contracted with Cyanamid to carry out excavation of Cyanamid's waste disposal site.  During excavation, buried chemicals were exposed.  The worker sued both L&N and Cyanamid for negligence in exposing him to chemical poisoning.  Cyanamid and L&N were both Schedule 1 employers, however L&N was no longer in business.  The Tribunal decided that the worker's exposure to chemicals could constitute a 'chance event' within s. 1(1)(a).  He could have suffered a personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment within s. 3(1).  The worker's right of action against his employer, L&N, would be taken away.  Regarding the worker's claim against Cyanamid, the Tribunal considered s. 8(1) and s. 9(1).  Cyanamid argued that the worker did not have an option under s. 8(1) to claim benefits or sue because s 9(1) deemed the worker to be an employee of Cyanamid.  However, the Tribunal decided that s. 9(1) is limited to situations where the contractor or subcontractor is not a Schedule 1 employer. Therefore, Cyanamid was a person 'other than his employer' to the worker and an option would exist under s. 8(1) if the worker's right of action were not taken away.  The Tribunal then considered the applicability of s 8(9).  It interpreted the words 'where the employees of both employers were in the course of their employment at the time of the happening of the injury' to mean the workers were in the course of their employment at the relevant time given the particular circumstances of alleged.  Contemporaneity was not required in this instance.  The workers were in the course of their employment at the relevant times, ie burial and exposure of the chemicals.  Thus the worker's cause of action was taken away by s. 8(9) of the Act.

DecKeywords: Derivative action; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (right to sue) (dependants); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendants applied for a determination of whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away against the defendants Pfahler and Latimer. The plaintiff was a schedule 1 employer who employed her husband as well as Pfahler and Latimer. A vehicle owned by Latimer and occupied by the plaintiff's husband and Pfahler was struck by a train. The Tribunal found that the plaintiff's action under s. 60 of the Family Law Reform Act was a derivative action. Since the plaintiff's husband and Pfahler were in the course of their employment the husband would have had no right of action against Pfahler. Therefore, the plaintiff also had no right of action against Pfahler. There was no evidence presented as to whether Latimer who was not present at the time of the accident, was in the course of his employment. The Tribunal reserved its decision concerning a right of action against Latimer for 60 days to allow the parties to decide whether to present more evidence, failing which the Tribunal would decide the matter on the available evidence. It was not necessary for the Tribunal to address the problem of the dual status of the plaintiff as a spouse of the worker and as his schedule 1 employer.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical literature)
DecSummary: The worker's widow applied for leave to appeal a decision of the WCB Appeal Board denying entitlement for a nickel miner's death by lung cancer.  On the issue of good reason to doubt the correctness of the decision, the Tribunal decided that, although a medical report did contain an adjudicative opinion, the Appeal Board did not rely on it conclusively, but rather relied primarily on another report linking the lung cancer to cigarette smoking.  Further, the Tribunal would not reconsider or re-evaluate the evidence since there was substantial evidence to support the Appeal Board's decision.  In addition, failure to apply the benefit of the doubt principles was not grounds to doubt correctness of the decision, since the evidence as to the possible causes of the cancer was not approximately equal in weight. On the issue of substantial new evidence, the Tribunal found that seven academic articles submitted were published prior to the Appeal Board hearing and in any event, they at most, aided the widow's theory, but did not establish that the disease resulted from conditions in the workplace. The Tribunal also stated that failure of the Appeal Board to consider a particular article on its own initiative did not mean that the Appeal Board erred or that there was necessarily good reason to doubt the correctness of the decision. Leave to appeal was denied.
